doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

chapter: Lou Rawls band, Alias and Jaco
title: Jaco Pastorius's sound and his short time in the band
summary: Montalbano describes Jaco's fretless bass, tapes people thought were a Rhodes or sped up, his arranging ideas and why he didn't last.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: He probably — did he have trouble fitting into being a bass player in the Lou Rawls band? What it took?
Not in my estimation. No. Other people in the band had problems with it.

You know. But no, again, it was a thrill beyond belief. And not because, he didn’t have any name then, I mean it wasn’t like the great Jaco Pastorius, it was just this phenomenal, incredible sound coming out of an electric bass, and you’re looking, is there something hooked up? I used to bring recordings of him back. I was taping all the time then. I had a little SONY cassette recorder and I taped everything. And it was the Watergate years. So I would bring tapes back and I remember playing for Sammy Mancuso and he would go “what? No. That’s a Fender Rhodes.” “No, no man, it’s a bass. It’s an electric bass.” “No.” Because he was doing the chords, you know, the harmonic stuff, all of that business. Then other people thought you sped up the tape. You know you played it in normal, like a human being, and then you sped up the tape to make it seem like he was playing so fast and all of that.
What was your take on how he got that sound? It seemed like even if he just played a couple of notes that he had that sound. Was he playing a fretless?

It was a fretless bass. As I recall it was, he made it a fretless bass. He took the frets off and filled them in and did all that. But it was an amplified sound, from his hands, the way he used his fingers and the way — it was him. That was his sound. It was like nothing in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-

those years, it was like nothing I’d ever heard before. I don’t think anyone had ever heard a sound like that. Not that I know of, coming out of a bass. It was just startling when you first hear it. And he was a great, great kid back then. We had a ball. We had so much fun and so many laughs, and Don and Jaco and myself, crazy stuff. Yeah. Nothing like where he ended up. Complete health nut, running, and sports you know, playing basketball and running all the time, and I couldn’t keep up with him you know.
That’s too bad. Did he play more than he needed on the gig? Is that why he didn’t last?

Again, not in my estimation, Monk. I may have a slightly skewed perspective because I was so in favor of him being in the band and wanting him to be out on the road with us, so maybe I overlooked something. But I don’t think so. I just think it was so different. No he played the music, he played it beautifully man. You know. He instantly could do the whole thing. No it wasn’t like he was soloing and playing crazy busy behind Lou or anything. Yeah, I think he caused a little fear in some people you know. And he had some ideas about rearranging Lou’s book. He was a great arranger you know, a great musical mind, at the piano and the whole thing, which was another thing I was looking forward to. Because by that time I was a little tired of playing that music the same way every night, and you know.
